reason: The provided sources from multiple independent sites confirm all key facts of Venera 13's survival, mission science, and post-mission controversies.
story: On March 1, 1982, the Soviet probe Venera 13 touched down on the hellish surface of Venus. Engineers designed the lander to survive only about 32 minutes before succumbing to the environment. The landing site was an inferno: surface temperatures reached 457 degrees Celsius—hot enough to melt lead—under crushing pressure 89 times greater than Earth's atmosphere. Yet Venera 13 defied expectations, transmitting data for 127 minutes. During more than two hours on the surface, it broadcast the first acoustic recording of another world, capturing the howl of Venusian winds. It extended a mechanical drill to extract and chemically analyze rock samples in an onboard chamber, and transmitted the first color panoramas of Venus's surface. Decades later, a Russian scientist claimed the photographs revealed living organisms, but independent experts proved the supposed creature was actually the probe's own discarded camera lens cap.
angle: A spacecraft designed to die in 32 minutes on a lead-melting, submarine-crushing world lasted over two hours, returned the first color photos and audio from another planet, and later had its own discarded lens cap mistaken for alien life.

claims.claim: Venera 13 touched down on the surface of Venus on 1 March 1982.
The Venera 13 lander was designed to function on the surface for approximately 32 minutes.
The lander survived and transmitted data for 127 minutes on the surface.
The surface temperature at the landing site was 457 degrees Celsius.
The atmospheric surface pressure at the landing site was 89 Earth atmospheres.
Venera 13 touched down east of Phoebe Regio at 7.5 degrees South, 303 degrees East.
Venera 13 sent back the first color photographs ever taken from the surface of Venus.
Venera 13 transmitted the first acoustic sound recordings ever made on another planet.
An onboard microphone was used to record atmospheric wind noise to estimate surface wind speed.
A mechanical drilling arm collected a Venusian surface soil sample.
The collected sample was stored and tested in an internal chamber held at 30 degrees Celsius and 0.05 atmospheres.
An onboard X-ray fluorescence spectrometer analyzed the mineral composition of the surface soil.
The soil sample was identified as a weakly differentiated melanocratic alkaline gabbroid rock.
Data was relayed from the lander back to Earth through a flyby bus spacecraft.
Russian scientist Leonid Ksanfomaliti claimed that objects in the Venera 13 images showed evidence of living creatures.
Image analysts identified the claimed moving organism on the surface as the lander's ejected camera lens cap.
Twin lander Venera 14 landed approximately 950 kilometers away from Venera 13.
On Venera 14, an ejected lens cap landed directly under the compressibility testing arm, causing it to measure the cap instead of the ground.

disputed: Descent mechanism: S1 claims the parachute detached at 50 kilometers and the lander completed descent using simple air braking, while S4 claims the lander rode its parachute all the way down. Script should state it plunged through the dense atmosphere without specifying parachute deployment depth.

Camera lens cap operation: S1 states that only one camera lens cap popped off successfully on Venera 13, whereas photo analysts cited in S5 and S7 indicate both opposite-facing cameras uncovered and took panoramic images. Script should refer to the panoramic imagery and ejected lens cap without asserting a camera failure.

Claims of Venusian life: Leonid Ksanfomaliti's claim of animal-like forms ('scorpion' and 'disc') was refuted by external experts as discarded lander components and digital image noise. Script must frame this as a debunked claim.
